notes.title: SoundSculpt: Direction and Semantics Driven Ambisonic Target Sound Extraction
notes.bp: A listener should be able to extract a selected sound from an ambisonic scene using both where it is and what it is.
notes.wh: The target direction is continuous while semantic cues are uncertain; spatial-only extraction can confuse co-located or reverberant sources and semantic-only cues ignore acoustic geometry.
notes.naive: Apply one fixed beamformer or condition a monaural extractor on a text label without modeling the multichannel sound field.
notes.ap: Condition an ambisonic-in/ambisonic-out extractor jointly on target direction and semantic embeddings, and test whether the cues complement one another.
notes.mech: The network maps multichannel ambisonic mixtures to a target sound field; direction and image-derived semantic embeddings guide the mask or representation used for extraction.
notes.math: Spatial filtering and semantic conditioning define complementary constraints: the output must preserve the target's spatial structure while suppressing other sources.
notes.eval: Spatial filtering and semantic conditioning define complementary constraints: the output must preserve the target's spatial structure while suppressing other sources.
notes.ww: SoundSculpt outperforms the reported signal-processing baselines on synthetic and real ambisonic mixtures, with joint spatial-semantic conditioning helping in difficult cases.
notes.limits: Synthetic scene construction, ambisonic order, semantic detector quality, room conditions, and target definition bound transfer; benchmark improvement is not guaranteed perceptual source isolation in arbitrary rooms.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Deep learning based spatial aliasing reduction in beamforming for audio capture
notes.bp: A microphone array should capture a desired direction without high-frequency spatial aliasing destroying beamformer accuracy.
notes.wh: Sparse or widely spaced arrays create directional ambiguity above the aliasing frequency, while an adaptive correction must preserve useful cross-channel phase and remain computationally practical.
notes.naive: Use a conventional beamformer unchanged, or apply a generic post-filter that ignores the array geometry and signal dependence.
notes.ap: Predict a signal-dependent de-aliasing filter with a U-Net and apply it to conventional beamforming, comparing independent-channel and cross-channel designs.
notes.mech: The model estimates a filter from multichannel spectro-temporal input; the corrected beamformer output is evaluated in common spatial-capture scenarios against conventional and learned alternatives.
notes.math: The learned filter approximates an inverse of geometry-induced aliasing, but its validity depends on the array and acoustic distribution represented during training.
notes.eval: The learned filter approximates an inverse of geometry-induced aliasing, but its validity depends on the array and acoustic distribution represented during training.
notes.ww: The paper reports reduced spatial aliasing and improved spatial/spectral capture measures for the proposed deep-learning correction in the tested scenarios.
notes.limits: Array geometry, source locations, reverberation, training mixtures, and scenario coverage constrain generalization; simulated or benchmark gains do not establish robustness for every microphone layout.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Revival with Voice: Multi-modal Controllable Text-to-Speech Synthesis
notes.bp: A controllable TTS system should synthesize a plausible voice from a face image and obey natural-language descriptions of speaking style and acoustic conditions.
notes.wh: Face-driven corpora are limited in audio quality, artistic portraits differ from real faces, and controls such as pace, distance, tone, and noise interact rather than forming independent knobs.
notes.naive: Train only on paired face-audio data and expose separate hand-tuned controls that do not generalize beyond the training corpus.
notes.ap: Augment face-driven training with high-quality audio-only speech, stylize face inputs to cover artistic portraits, and condition synthesis on natural-language control descriptions.
notes.mech: The face encoder supplies speaker or voice information, while text conditioning specifies controllable attributes; multi-modal training aligns these conditions with waveform generation.
notes.math: The system treats identity and controllable acoustic attributes as separate but compositional conditioning variables, evaluated through speech quality, similarity, and control-following tests.
notes.eval: The system treats identity and controllable acoustic attributes as separate but compositional conditioning variables, evaluated through speech quality, similarity, and control-following tests.
notes.ww: Revival with Voice reports controllable synthesis from real and artistic face inputs and improved use of high-quality audio-only data in the tested settings.
notes.limits: Face distribution, language, control wording, subjective protocol, and disentanglement assumptions limit the claim; controllability is not proof of identity fidelity or safe use of a person's likeness.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Vocoder-Projected Feature Discriminator
notes.bp: Waveform-generating models need an adversarial signal that rewards perceptual detail without making training prohibitively expensive.
notes.wh: Time-domain discrimination after waveform upsampling consumes memory and computation, while compact acoustic features can hide artifacts that appear after vocoding.
notes.naive: Discriminate only mel or acoustic features, or run a full waveform discriminator at every training step despite the cost.
notes.ap: Project generated acoustic features through a vocoder and discriminate in a vocoder-feature space, retaining waveform-relevant feedback with lower time-domain overhead.
notes.mech: The vocoder-projected feature discriminator compares feature representations after synthesis; diffusion-based voice-conversion distillation tests whether the adversarial target improves the generated waveform.
notes.math: The discriminator changes the metric space rather than the generator's output target: it seeks features that preserve vocoder-relevant waveform distinctions while avoiding repeated raw-waveform processing.
notes.eval: The discriminator changes the metric space rather than the generator's output target: it seeks features that preserve vocoder-relevant waveform distinctions while avoiding repeated raw-waveform processing.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved diffusion-based VC distillation quality from the projected-feature discriminator under the evaluated settings.
notes.limits: Vocoder choice, feature projection, training compute, VC data, and perceptual evaluation determine the result; a reported quality gain does not establish universal TTS or VC superiority.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: A Multi-Dialectal Dataset for German Dialect ASR and Dialect-to-Standard Speech Translation
notes.bp: Speech technology should measure and translate German dialect variation rather than treating Standard German as the only valid target.
notes.wh: Dialect differences affect both acoustic realization and lexical/transcription conventions, and models can appear accurate while erasing the variety in translation to Standard German.
notes.naive: Train or evaluate only on Standard German and assume the resulting error and translation behavior represent all German speakers.
notes.ap: Create a multi-dialect benchmark with dialectal and Standard German transcriptions, then compare multilingual ASR systems on recognition and dialect-to-standard speech translation.
notes.mech: The dataset crosses three Southeast German dialect groups and Standard German; paired transcription conventions make both recognition fidelity and normalization visible.
notes.math: Dialect identity is a structured source of variation, not merely noise: evaluation can distinguish preserving dialect words from mapping them to a standardized target.
notes.eval: Dialect identity is a structured source of variation, not merely noise: evaluation can distinguish preserving dialect words from mapping them to a standardized target.
notes.ww: Betthupferl provides four hours of dialect speech plus Standard German and reports model-dependent differences in recognition and translation behavior across dialect groups.
notes.limits: Read speech, regional coverage, speaker sampling, benchmark size, and translation direction constrain the conclusions; dataset inclusion does not guarantee broad fairness or dialect preservation in deployed systems.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Audio-Based Classification and Geographic Regression of Austrian Dialects
notes.bp: An acoustic model should identify regional dialect variation without simply memorizing the speaker identity or location-specific recording conditions.
notes.wh: Dialect and speaker cues are entangled, locations are unevenly sampled, and geographic regression requires a continuous notion of error rather than a single class label.
notes.naive: Train a classifier on pooled speech and interpret speaker memorization as dialect recognition, or predict only coarse dialect groups.
notes.ap: Use speaker augmentation to reduce speaker-specific bias and jointly examine dialect/location classification with geographic-coordinate regression.
notes.mech: The model learns speech representations for hierarchical classification and a continuous coordinate prediction; held-out speaker and location splits test whether regional structure survives identity variation.
notes.math: Classification partitions a geographic continuum while regression measures distance in kilometers, so the two tasks expose different resolutions and failure modes of dialect modeling.
notes.eval: Classification partitions a geographic continuum while regression measures distance in kilometers, so the two tasks expose different resolutions and failure modes of dialect modeling.
notes.ww: The Austrian dataset covers 304 speakers at 108 locations; wav2vec 2.0 reports an average geographic test error of 66.7 km in the paper's evaluation.
notes.limits: Sampling density, speaker augmentation, Austrian dialect geography, split design, and recording conditions limit transfer; geographic prediction is not a complete sociolinguistic account of dialect.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Adversarial Deep Metric Learning for Cross-Modal Audio-Text Alignment in Open-Vocabulary Keyword Spotting
notes.bp: Text-enrolled keyword spotting should recognize a word not seen as a fixed acoustic class by aligning an utterance with its text description.
notes.wh: Audio and text embeddings have different modality statistics; a shared space can match superficial modality cues instead of phonetic or lexical content.
notes.naive: Compare audio and text embeddings directly with ordinary metric learning and assume the modality gap disappears with more data.
notes.ap: Adversarially train a modality classifier so audio and text encoders produce modality-invariant embeddings, then optimize deep metric alignment for open-vocabulary KWS.
notes.mech: The encoders map acoustic queries and text enrollments into a shared space; the adversarial classifier penalizes recoverable modality identity while the metric objective pulls matched keyword pairs together.
notes.math: The shared embedding is a constrained retrieval geometry: matched audio/text pairs should be close, while modality identity should be uninformative to the adversary.
notes.eval: The shared embedding is a constrained retrieval geometry: matched audio/text pairs should be close, while modality identity should be uninformative to the adversary.
notes.ww: Modality-invariant alignment improves the audio-text retrieval decision used for unseen-keyword spotting in the reported experiments.
notes.limits: Vocabulary, languages, negative sampling, enrollment text, threshold calibration, and speaker/channel variation bound the claim; open-vocabulary benchmark accuracy is not unrestricted lexical understanding.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Word Level Timestamp Generation for Automatic Speech Recognition and Translation
notes.bp: Speech recognition and translation systems need word boundaries and timestamps for retrieval, subtitles, and downstream editing without a separate forced-aligner at inference time.
notes.wh: Timestamp prediction must preserve word order while generating content, and errors in one boundary can shift every later timestamp.
notes.naive: Attach an external aligner after decoding or force the sequence model to emit timestamps without a training signal for their timing semantics.
notes.ap: Use a forced aligner as a teacher to create timestamp supervision, add a timestamp token, and train the end-to-end Canary model to emit start and end times with words.
notes.mech: Teacher-generated word intervals become sequence targets; the model's timestamp tokens interleave with recognized or translated content, allowing boundary prediction inside the decoder.
notes.math: Alignment quality is measured against teacher or reference timing and downstream recognition/translation behavior, testing whether an integrated decoder can replace a separate alignment stage.
notes.eval: Alignment quality is measured against teacher or reference timing and downstream recognition/translation behavior, testing whether an integrated decoder can replace a separate alignment stage.
notes.ww: The paper reports word-level timestamp generation for Canary with the proposed token and teacher-supervised training in the evaluated ASR/translation settings.
notes.limits: Teacher timing quality, tokenization, language, speaking rate, and evaluation alignment constrain transfer; timestamp agreement does not by itself prove subtitle readability or translation quality.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.
